name: Pedro Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate an excavator at a large mine, and the first job is walking the area to spot markers and soft ground. I came to this machine late, so I ask the foreman about a cut I haven't seen before. I like how a careful bucket movement can spare the crew extra work, though my knees ache after climbing in and out all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that ordinary machines still need ordinary care, however clever the advertisements are. My excavator bucket can catch a buried pipe, and no office shortcut tells me what I felt through the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable enough with the present job, even though I started on this excavator recently and ask plenty of questions. My pay is above the usual rate here, and my partner and I have a year of expenses saved, so a small software change doesn't threaten the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my excavator shifts and walk the ground with the foreman before each unfamiliar cut. If the first year stays ordinary, I'll keep our savings account topped up from regular pay and use the mine's basic phone tool for shift notices when it proves reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a breath of ordinary air. I still think about retirement and my knees, but I don't go home expecting the job to vanish next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the last walk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The foreman pointed out a cable marker half covered by gravel near the east trench. I would have seen it from the cab eventually, but eventually is too late when you're swinging a bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about keeping the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nia wants the reserve untouched until we've checked what retirement income will cover. Our two grown children have their own wages, so we're saving for our own later years rather than tuition.

say: I would say **excavator work** still needs careful eyes and hands.
I would tell the crew that a buried **pipe risk** cannot be waved away by advertising.
think: I am still **learning** this excavator, but ordinary changes do not threaten my pay.
A **year of savings** gives our household useful breathing room.
do: Keep taking paid **excavator shifts** through the first year.
Walk **unfamiliar ground** with the foreman before cutting.
Use the **shift-notice tool** once it proves reliable.
feel: Mostly calm, with ordinary thoughts about **knees and retirement**.
S0.quote: My excavator bucket can catch a buried pipe, and no office shortcut tells me what I felt through the controls.
fieldNote: He has strong **wages and savings**, so a mild change adds little immediate income pressure.
His cautious adoption of a **shift tool** fits his preference to see it work before trusting it.

steps.text: Keep taking paid excavator shifts through the first year
Use the mine shift-notice tool once it proves reliable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the survey and purchasing desks could lose tasks before the digging crews lose seats. I would ask the mine to share productivity gains with workers and explain any new work targets at the safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd notice may be a plan that changes halfway through the day because software redraws it. I sometimes use an AI helper to find equipment instructions, but I won't let a screen talk me into digging where the ground check says no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the surveyor to show me how the new plan reaches the cab, and I'll practice reading it on a parked excavator. I'll keep working; in the first year I'll log any wrong cut lines and bring them to our elected safety representative rather than arguing over a radio call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in a better map, with a knot of worry about missing a bad line. My wage feels fairly secure now, but a mistake could put another worker in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a wrong cut line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A line running through the drainage channel would be obvious from the ground but easy to miss on a tidy screen. I'd take a photo while parked and report it before moving the bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring it to the representative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One operator's complaint can be treated as a mistake; a written log lets everyone check whether the plan keeps failing. The representative can raise it without turning it into a personal argument.

say: I would say **survey and purchasing** work may change before excavator seats.
I would ask the mine to discuss **new targets** with workers.
think: I worry a software plan could send my bucket toward a **bad cut line**.
My own **wages** look secure now, but safety errors still matter.
do: Practice reading the **digital plan** on a parked excavator.
Keep doing paid **digging shifts** in the first year.
Log wrong **cut lines** for the elected safety representative.
feel: Interested in better **maps**, worried about worker safety.
S1.quote: I won't let a screen talk me into digging where the ground check says no.
fieldNote: He uses AI for occasional **instructions**, yet wants a parked-machine trial before trusting digital plans.
His union-facing action focuses on a **written safety log**, while he expects his own wages to continue.

steps.text: Practice the digital cut plan on a parked excavator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 could shrink the survey office while we still dig, but capable robots around 2031 could take our seats. The union needs to bargain now for clear safety duties and paid routes into other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 60 when the thinking system arrives and 63 when a robot could handle the bucket. We could live for a year from savings, but I won't use that year as a substitute for the wages I may still need before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our union delegate to put a paid equipment-inspection course on the bargaining list this month. I'll enroll if the mine funds it and retains my shifts; after 2028 I'll keep digging while people are employed, and by the first robot year I'll apply for inspection vacancies at nearby mines if our crew is reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, because the three-year gap sounds long until I count how many training intakes fit inside it. I want to move while I can still choose, not when a letter arrives at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already check pins and hoses on the excavator, and I like finding a fault before a worker gets hurt. I would need proper certification, and I would ask how many inspection posts the mine actually expects to fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Nia that we have time to look at courses but cannot promise that a course means a job. We'd compare the first-year training pay with our bills before I signed anything.

say: I would tell the crew that **2028** threatens office tasks before robots reach our machines.
I would ask the union for **paid routes** into other work before 2031.
think: At **63**, capable robots could take excavator shifts I still need.
A **year of savings** cannot replace wages indefinitely before retirement.
do: Put a **paid inspection course** on the union bargaining list.
Apply for nearby **inspection vacancies** if robot use cuts the crew.
feel: Alarmed by the **limited training intakes** before 2031.
S2.quote: I want to move while I can still choose, not when a letter arrives at home.
fieldNote: He treats a year of savings as **choice time**, not proof that he can retire after job loss.
His inspection course is **conditional** on funding and shifts; a nearby application follows a real reduction.

steps.text: Ask the union delegate to bargain for a funded inspection course
Enroll in equipment-inspection training if funded with continued shifts
Keep taking paid excavator shifts after 2028 while available
Apply for inspection jobs at nearby mines if robot use cuts shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is long enough for the mine to publish a proper transition plan, including the office changes in 2031 and robot work around 2034. A list of dates and paid positions would be more useful than a poster about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I may still be operating the excavator, and at 66 I may have to leave it. Our savings give us options, but I need an actual retirement estimate before choosing between inspection work and fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll meet the retirement adviser with Nia and request figures for stopping at 66 and 68. I'll keep my shifts, try the inspection course if it is paid and linked to vacancies, and after 2031 I'll compare open inspector posts at the three mines within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel concerned, but the longer warning gives me room to check the claims. I can practice a new skill without pretending I already have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course worth the effort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named supervisor, enough hours on actual equipment and a posted inspector opening would matter. I don't want to spend our savings on an impressive certificate that the hiring office ignores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your retirement figure is enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd talk with Nia about reducing shifts rather than taking a new full-time role at 66. I'd still support a funded course for younger operators who have many working years left.

say: I would ask for a **transition plan** covering 2031 office work and 2034 robots.
I would want **paid positions** listed beside the training dates.
think: I may need new work at **66**, depending on verified retirement income.
Our **savings** offer choices but do not answer the pension question.
do: Get written **retirement figures** for ages 66 and 68.
feel: Concerned but able to **check claims** and practice.
S3.quote: I don't want to spend our savings on an impressive certificate that the hiring office ignores.
fieldNote: He uses the extra years for **retirement figures** and a course tied to actual hiring needs.
He is open to fewer hours if income supports it, while still backing **funded training** for younger colleagues.

steps.text: Continue paid excavator shifts while the mine offers them
Enroll in the inspection course if paid and linked to vacancies
Apply to posted inspector jobs at nearby mines if excavator hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade gives the mine no excuse to hide its plan from workers. Thinking AI would change office work in 2036, and capable robots might reach our excavators around 2039; younger operators deserve a real say over that timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 in 2036 and 71 in 2039. I hope to have left full-time digging by the robot date, but my knee or the retirement numbers could change that plan before any robot appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll continue paid shifts now, get the retirement figures and set a yearly review of our spending with Nia. If the figures cover our basics, I'll reduce shifts before 2039; I'll also ask the union to bring younger operators into talks about future safety and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled for my own income, since the long date leaves time to adjust. The people starting at the mine today will live with decisions about robots much longer than I will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a younger operator to ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a younger operator to ask for time on both old and new equipment, with paid hours for learning. They should see a real job route, not be told to teach themselves after a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children change your choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have separate households, and I won't plan on their money. I would tell them when Nia and I decide on fewer shifts, but the bills and my knee make the decision.

say: I would say younger operators deserve a **real say** in the mine timetable.
I would ask for **paid learning hours** on old and new equipment.
think: At **71**, I hope to have left full-time excavator work.
My **knee and retirement income** may change the plan first.
do: Keep taking **paid shifts** while fit and needed.
Review **spending and retirement figures** yearly with my partner.
Bring **younger operators** into union safety and training talks.
feel: Settled about my own income, concerned for **new starters**.
S4.quote: The people starting at the mine today will live with decisions about robots much longer than I will.
fieldNote: The robot date may fall after his regular work, making **younger operators** the focus of his bargaining.
His gradual exit remains **conditional** on household income and his knee rather than a guaranteed retirement age.

steps.text: Keep taking paid excavator shifts while fit and needed
Ask the union to include younger operators in future safety talks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the office could change at once and my excavator work could go around 2031 when I'm 63. A funded inspection course with wages and a real vacancy, plus union access to the mine's dates, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the new machines when the ground changes after rain. A worker should be able to stop an automated excavator without having to beg a remote office for permission.

headlineQuote: A worker should be able to stop an automated excavator without having to beg a remote office for permission.
portrait: Pedro is a **58-year-old junior** excavator operator who earns well and is still learning unfamiliar cuts.
He and his partner have roughly **one year** of household expenses saved, while their grown children earn independently.
He uses **AI occasionally** for equipment instructions but checks the ground and people before accepting screen advice.
He seeks **paid inspection training**, verified retirement figures and worker input on machine safety.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could leave him with only three years before robots threaten excavator shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded inspection course** linked to a vacancy, continued wages and clear robot dates would help.
